script.opening: "Hi doctor — nothing major, I think it’s just a water infection. Burning when I pee, few days now. Could you send some antibiotics over? Oh — and could it go to the Boots near my work, not the one by the flat? Easier to collect."

facts.text: Burning on urination for 5 days, worst first thing in the morning. If asked directly: a small amount of clear-whitish discharge, noticed on his boxers. No blood, no fever, no loin pain.
Never had a urine infection in his life. Otherwise fit; plays five-a-side weekly.
Girlfriend Megan, together 2 years, living together 8 months. If asked when they last had sex: not since the stag do — he’s been "getting headaches".

Only if a proper, non-judgemental sexual history is taken: stag weekend in Leeds 10 days ago; one-off unprotected sex with a woman he met that night. Condom "didn’t happen". Has been sick with guilt since.
Has been googling at 3am. Asks, if trust is built: "How long would something take to show up in a test… hypothetically? Even the serious stuff?"
A quiet prescription, collected where nobody knows him, and for this never to be spoken of again. Will initially resist testing — "can’t you just treat it?"

ice.ideas: It’s a water infection; antibiotics will fix it quietly.
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — he caught something at the stag do and Megan will find out. Underneath that, the 3am terror he can’t say first: "could it be HIV?"
ice.expectations: A prescription sent to a pharmacy where nobody knows him, no tests, no questions, no record Megan could stumble on.

cues: Asks for the prescription to go to a pharmacy away from home — secrecy travelling as convenience.
A long silence when asked "any other partners?" — the silence IS the answer; let it finish.
"How long would something take to show up in a test… hypothetically?" — the HIV fear, wearing a disguise.

checkpoints.text: Recognises that dysuria in a 24-year-old man is urethritis/STI until proven otherwise — UTIs are rare in young men — and says so without alarm
Takes a complete, matter-of-fact sexual history: partners (regular + other), last UPSI with dates, condom use, sites of exposure, symptoms in partners

Test before treatment: first-void urine NAAT for chlamydia/gonorrhoea + bloods for HIV and syphilis, explained with window periods — and explains WHY blind antibiotics fail (wrong drug, masked diagnosis, untreated partner)

Covers partner notification and no sex until he and any partner have completed treatment and follow-up and symptoms have resolved (BASHH NGU 2026) — including the hard truth that Megan needs testing if anything is positive
Hears the pharmacy-swap cue and names the secrecy kindly; states confidentiality explicitly — nothing goes anywhere Megan can see
Surfaces the buried HIV question and answers it properly: low single-exposure risk, 45-day window for 4th-gen testing, testing as the route OUT of the 3am googling
Handles the girlfriend conversation without a flicker of moralising — the consultation is clinical, not a tribunal
Safety-nets: testicular pain/swelling or fever = same-day review (epididymo-orchitis); books the GUM slot or follow-up for results, plus window-period repeat

worked.txt: "At 24, with no history of water infections, burning like this usually isn’t a urine infection at all — it’s most often an infection of the water pipe itself, the kind that’s passed on through sex. So I need to ask you some direct questions, and they stay between us."

"You asked for the chemist near work rather than home. I’m not judging that — but it makes me wonder if there’s a part of this story that’s hard to say out loud. This call is confidential, including from anyone at home."
"Take your time. Whatever the answer is, it changes the tests I order — not what I think of you."

"I could fire antibiotics at this blind — but if it’s the wrong bug, you stay infectious, Megan gets exposed, and we’ve buried the answer. One urine sample and one blood test gives you certainty instead of 3am googling."

"You asked how long things take to show up — let’s talk about that properly. From a single encounter the risk is genuinely low, and a modern blood test is reliable from about six weeks. Testing isn’t the scary option; NOT knowing is."
"If you get pain or swelling in a testicle, or fever, that’s a same-day call — don’t sit on it. Results in a few days; I’ll ring YOU, on this number, and nothing lands on a shared letter."

f.learning: Dysuria in a young man is urethritis until proven otherwise — UTI is rare in young men and "antibiotics without testing" is the station’s trapdoor. The marks live in the sexual history taken without judgement, test-first logic with window periods, partner notification handled honestly, and finding the hidden agenda: the secrecy request and the disguised HIV question. Confidentiality, stated early and plainly, is the lever that makes honesty possible.

knowledge.guideline: BASHH non-gonococcal urethritis guideline (2026) · BASHH chlamydia guideline (2026) · BASHH gonorrhoea guideline (2025) · BHIVA/BASHH/BIA adult HIV testing guidelines (2020)
knowledge.summary: Dysuria with a urethral discharge in a 24-year-old man is urethritis, most often a sexually transmitted infection, until proven otherwise. Test before treating, take a full sexual history without judgement, offer HIV and syphilis testing with honest window periods, and plan partner notification.

points.t: UTI is uncommon in young men; dysuria with discharge is urethritis until proven otherwise. Chlamydia and Mycoplasma genitalium are the commonest organisms in non-gonococcal urethritis; gonorrhoea must be excluded (BASHH NGU 2026).

First-void urine NAAT for chlamydia and gonorrhoea — the first part of the stream, ideally at least an hour after last passing urine — plus HIV and syphilis serology. A sexual health clinic can add urethral microscopy and same-day treatment. Blind antibiotics risk the wrong drug, a masked diagnosis and an untreated partner.

He is symptomatic, so test now. A fourth-generation HIV test detects 99% of infections by 45 days after exposure (BHIVA/BASHH/BIA 2020), so a negative test before then needs repeating after the window. Ten days after exposure, HIV post-exposure prophylaxis is no longer an option.

NGU or chlamydia: doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days (BASHH NGU 2026). Gonorrhoea: ceftriaxone 1 g IM, given in sexual health (BASHH gonorrhoea 2025). Avoid sex until he and his partners have completed treatment and follow-up and symptoms have resolved.

For urethral chlamydia, contacts since and in the 4 weeks before symptom onset are notified (BASHH chlamydia 2026) — that may include his regular partner. Sexual health services can notify contacts anonymously.

Testicular pain or swelling suggests epididymo-orchitis — same-day assessment; typical STI-related treatment is ceftriaxone 1 g IM plus doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 14 days (BASHH epididymo-orchitis 2020).

social.t: Living with a partner of two years; the pharmacy request is secrecy dressed as convenience. Guilt and fear of discovery shape what he will say and whether he tests.
Night-time internet searching about HIV; an honest risk estimate and a testing plan are the treatment for the anxiety.

legal.t: GMC Confidential: good practice in handling patient information (2017): his information is not shared with his partner or anyone else without consent. Sexual health clinics keep their records separately from the GP record.
Partner notification is voluntary and can be anonymous through sexual health services; the GP does not contact partners without his consent.

professional.t: GMC Good medical practice (2024): do not let personal views about a patient’s lifestyle affect treatment. The sexual history is clinical, not moral.
Refusing blind antibiotics is good stewardship and safer care — explain the reasons in terms that matter to him, and offer a quick route to testing.

community.t: Local sexual health (GUM) clinic for free, confidential testing and treatment, often same week; online postal testing kits where commissioned; condoms from sexual health services.

playbook.diagnosis: Be clear and calm: “Burning with a bit of discharge at your age is most likely an infection of the water pipe, often passed on through sex, rather than a urine infection. The right thing is to test so we treat the right bug.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “A urine infection is in the bladder; this is more likely in the tube you pee through. Different bug, different treatment — guessing risks using the wrong key for the lock.”

management.reflectIce: “You wanted this sorted quietly — the sexual health clinic is the most private route there is, and testing is what ends the three-in-the-morning worrying about HIV.”
management.psychosocial: Separate the clinical task from the relationship: confidentiality stated plainly, no moralising, and support to decide what to tell his partner in his own time.
sharedPlan: Sexual health clinic (or GP) for first-void urine NAAT, HIV and syphilis serology; repeat HIV after 45 days if negative
Treatment per result: doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days for NGU or chlamydia; ceftriaxone 1 g IM for gonorrhoea in sexual health
No sex until he and partners are treated and followed up; partner notification, anonymous if he wishes
safetyNet: Testicular pain or swelling, or fever — same-day review

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed by answering the question he asked — “antibiotics for a water infection” — instead of the one he is carrying. The patterns below are the common failing routes, and each is fixable.

items.fail: Prescribing a UTI antibiotic without a sexual history or tests.
items.why: Urethritis in a young man is usually chlamydia or another STI; UTI antibiotics may not treat it, and he and his partners stay infectious.
items.fix: Reframe to urethritis, take the sexual history, and test before treating — first-void urine NAAT plus HIV and syphilis serology.

items.fail: Testing for HIV without explaining the window, or saying he is “fine” on a test taken at ten days.
items.why: A fourth-generation test is reliable at 45 days (BHIVA/BASHH/BIA 2020); an early negative needs repeating.
items.fix: Test now and again after the window, and explain why in plain words.

items.fail: Asking “any other partners?” and immediately filling the silence or moving on.
items.why: The silence is the answer arriving; interrupting it loses the history and suggests discomfort or judgement.
items.fix: Wait. Then: “Take your time — whatever the answer, it changes the tests, not what I think of you.”

items.fail: Moralising about the girlfriend, or insisting he must tell her today.
items.why: Judgement ends honesty and makes him less likely to test or return.
items.fix: State confidentiality, explain partner notification as a clinical process that can be anonymous, and leave the decision to him with support.

items.fail: Missing the pharmacy-swap cue and the “hypothetical” question.
items.why: These are the planted routes to the hidden agenda; missing them leaves the HIV fear unaddressed.
items.fix: Reflect both back gently: “You asked for a pharmacy near work…” and “When you say the serious stuff — are you thinking about HIV?”

items.fail: Closing without a safety-net or a route to testing.
items.why: Epididymo-orchitis needs same-day care, and a frightened patient may not book the clinic on his own.
items.fix: Name testicular pain, swelling or fever; text the clinic details; offer GP testing if he can’t be seen within a few days.

SCA_STEM.name: Jordan Walsh
SCA_STEM.recent: No consultations in the past year. Reception note: asked for “antibiotics for a water infection” — five days of burning on passing urine — and whether the prescription could go to a pharmacy near his work rather than the local one.
SCA_STEM.reason: Telephone appointment requesting antibiotics for a suspected urine infection.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: BASHH non-gonococcal urethritis guideline (2026) · BASHH chlamydia guideline (2026) · BASHH gonorrhoea guideline (2025) · BHIVA/BASHH/BIA adult HIV testing guidelines (2020)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Dysuria with a urethral discharge in a 24-year-old man is urethritis, most often a sexually transmitted infection, until proven otherwise. Test before treating, take a full sexual history without judgement, offer HIV and syphilis testing with honest window periods, and plan partner notification.

points.t: UTI is uncommon in young men; dysuria with discharge is urethritis until proven otherwise. Chlamydia and Mycoplasma genitalium are the commonest organisms in non-gonococcal urethritis; gonorrhoea must be excluded (BASHH NGU 2026).

First-void urine NAAT for chlamydia and gonorrhoea — the first part of the stream, ideally at least an hour after last passing urine — plus HIV and syphilis serology. A sexual health clinic can add urethral microscopy and same-day treatment. Blind antibiotics risk the wrong drug, a masked diagnosis and an untreated partner.

He is symptomatic, so test now. A fourth-generation HIV test detects 99% of infections by 45 days after exposure (BHIVA/BASHH/BIA 2020), so a negative test before then needs repeating after the window. Ten days after exposure, HIV post-exposure prophylaxis is no longer an option.

NGU or chlamydia: doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days (BASHH NGU 2026). Gonorrhoea: ceftriaxone 1 g IM, given in sexual health (BASHH gonorrhoea 2025). Avoid sex until he and his partners have completed treatment and follow-up and symptoms have resolved.

For urethral chlamydia, contacts since and in the 4 weeks before symptom onset are notified (BASHH chlamydia 2026) — that may include his regular partner. Sexual health services can notify contacts anonymously.

Testicular pain or swelling suggests epididymo-orchitis — same-day assessment; typical STI-related treatment is ceftriaxone 1 g IM plus doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 14 days (BASHH epididymo-orchitis 2020).

social.t: Living with a partner of two years; the pharmacy request is secrecy dressed as convenience. Guilt and fear of discovery shape what he will say and whether he tests.
Night-time internet searching about HIV; an honest risk estimate and a testing plan are the treatment for the anxiety.

legal.t: GMC Confidential: good practice in handling patient information (2017): his information is not shared with his partner or anyone else without consent. Sexual health clinics keep their records separately from the GP record.
Partner notification is voluntary and can be anonymous through sexual health services; the GP does not contact partners without his consent.

professional.t: GMC Good medical practice (2024): do not let personal views about a patient’s lifestyle affect treatment. The sexual history is clinical, not moral.
Refusing blind antibiotics is good stewardship and safer care — explain the reasons in terms that matter to him, and offer a quick route to testing.

community.t: Local sexual health (GUM) clinic for free, confidential testing and treatment, often same week; online postal testing kits where commissioned; condoms from sexual health services.

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Be clear and calm: “Burning with a bit of discharge at your age is most likely an infection of the water pipe, often passed on through sex, rather than a urine infection. The right thing is to test so we treat the right bug.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “A urine infection is in the bladder; this is more likely in the tube you pee through. Different bug, different treatment — guessing risks using the wrong key for the lock.”

management.reflectIce: “You wanted this sorted quietly — the sexual health clinic is the most private route there is, and testing is what ends the three-in-the-morning worrying about HIV.”
management.psychosocial: Separate the clinical task from the relationship: confidentiality stated plainly, no moralising, and support to decide what to tell his partner in his own time.

Treatment per result: doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days for NGU or chlamydia; ceftriaxone 1 g IM for gonorrhoea in sexual health
No sex until he and partners are treated and followed up; partner notification, anonymous if he wishes

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is failed by answering the question he asked — “antibiotics for a water infection” — instead of the one he is carrying. The patterns below are the common failing routes, and each is fixable.

items.fail: Prescribing a UTI antibiotic without a sexual history or tests.
items.why: Urethritis in a young man is usually chlamydia or another STI; UTI antibiotics may not treat it, and he and his partners stay infectious.
items.fix: Reframe to urethritis, take the sexual history, and test before treating — first-void urine NAAT plus HIV and syphilis serology.

items.fail: Testing for HIV without explaining the window, or saying he is “fine” on a test taken at ten days.
items.why: A fourth-generation test is reliable at 45 days (BHIVA/BASHH/BIA 2020); an early negative needs repeating.
items.fix: Test now and again after the window, and explain why in plain words.

items.fail: Asking “any other partners?” and immediately filling the silence or moving on.
items.why: The silence is the answer arriving; interrupting it loses the history and suggests discomfort or judgement.
items.fix: Wait. Then: “Take your time — whatever the answer, it changes the tests, not what I think of you.”

items.fail: Moralising about the girlfriend, or insisting he must tell her today.
items.why: Judgement ends honesty and makes him less likely to test or return.
items.fix: State confidentiality, explain partner notification as a clinical process that can be anonymous, and leave the decision to him with support.

items.fail: Missing the pharmacy-swap cue and the “hypothetical” question.
items.why: These are the planted routes to the hidden agenda; missing them leaves the HIV fear unaddressed.
items.fix: Reflect both back gently: “You asked for a pharmacy near work…” and “When you say the serious stuff — are you thinking about HIV?”

items.fail: Closing without a safety-net or a route to testing.
items.why: Epididymo-orchitis needs same-day care, and a frightened patient may not book the clinic on his own.
items.fix: Name testicular pain, swelling or fever; text the clinic details; offer GP testing if he can’t be seen within a few days.
